summary: Reports on the STRINT workshop, where about a hundred participants met in London in early 2014 to discuss how the IETF and W3C should respond to pervasive monitoring. Topics included terminology, user interfaces, mitigation classes and opportunistic encryption.

plainLanguage.summary: Lots of experts got together to decide how to make the Internet harder to spy on.

questions: how should the ietf respond to pervasive monitoring
what did the strint workshop recommend about user interfaces
subtitle: How to strengthen the Internet against mass surveillance

tldr.problem: Pervasive monitoring, the large-scale collection of internet traffic and metadata by state and non-state actors, undermines privacy, freedom, and trust. Technical solutions alone are insufficient without policy changes and better user interfaces.
tldr.mechanism: The workshop brought together cryptographers, policy experts, engineers, and civil society to discuss concrete mitigations including stronger cryptography, opportunistic encryption, metadata minimization, traffic analysis countermeasures, and changes to how standards bodies operate.
tldr.outcome: The resulting recommendations shaped years of follow-up work, including new RFCs on opportunistic security, pervasive attack threat models, and better integration of security and privacy into standards development.

today: RFC 7687 is an Informational RFC reporting on a 2014 workshop. The recommendations have shaped follow-up work including RFC 7258 (Pervasive Monitoring Is an Attack), RFC 7435 (Opportunistic Security), and RFC 7624 (a threat model for surveillance). The IETF continues to integrate privacy and security into standards development.

sections.title: Context and Goals
sections.content: The STRINT workshop took place in London in March 2014, just before IETF 89, with 100 on-site participants and 165 more listening to streaming audio. It brought together standards experts, cryptographers, security researchers, policy makers, and civil society representatives around the central premise that pervasive monitoring is an attack, following IETF consensus established at IETF 88. The workshop examined what the IETF, W3C, and other standards bodies should do in response, and what broader actions (technical, policy, and social) could help strengthen the internet against surveillance.
sections.plainLanguage: A hundred experts met in London to talk about mass spying on the internet and what to do about it. They agreed that spying is a bad thing and worth fighting against.

sections.title: Key Recommendations
sections.content: The workshop produced 11 high-level recommendations. Encryption works well if implemented correctly, but trust is hard: the certificate system has been weakened by the ability of compromised certificate authorities to impersonate any domain. Alternatives discussed included certificate transparency (a public log of who issued which certificate), the web of trust model used by PGP, and trust on first use (TOFU) as employed by SSH. Traffic analysis (the study of who talks to whom and for how long) is less well understood but equally important: even encrypted messages leak metadata that can reveal the sender's identity and intent. The workshop recommended work on data minimization, padding, and multipath routing to make metadata harder to harvest. Opportunistic Security emerged as a key concept: adding encryption automatically when both endpoints can support it, falling back to cleartext only when necessary. A glossary definition was needed because the term was being used inconsistently across the community.
sections.plainLanguage: Strong secret codes work, but getting people to use them is hard. Even if messages are secret, the list of who sent to whom is still visible and still dangerous. When both people can use secret codes, they should use them automatically without asking.

sections.title: Understanding Threats and Mitigations
sections.content:
The workshop distinguished pervasive monitoring (PM) from traditional threat models. A PM attacker has no specific targets and simply collects everything, which changes the economics: a PM attacker is indifferent to cost or even prefers high costs. Authenticating an endpoint does not prevent a man-in-the-middle attack but makes it visible. An attacker must be present on every connection, and a key mismatch exposes the tampering.

The workshop also distinguished explicit metadata (ratings, provenance, copyright data) from implicit metadata (destination address, size, timing). New protocols should avoid leaking implicit metadata, and applications should minimize collection of explicit metadata. Fingerprinting, the process of identifying a client from patterns in its messages, was recognized as a privacy risk. Designers should mitigate this by reducing optional features and redundant data.
sections.plainLanguage: Big spies do not care about your secret. They just want to know who talks to whom. Hiding that is much harder than hiding the words. Even if you encrypt messages, the size and timing of messages can give away what you are doing, and people can recognize your patterns.

sections.title: Policy, Users, and Implementation
sections.content:
The workshop recognized that technical solutions alone cannot succeed without policy and social change. The public generally wants more privacy but is pessimistic about getting it. Government surveillance, justified by terrorism concerns, has expanded beyond what was previously acceptable. Standards bodies could institute ethics reviews for standards like the Geolocation API and document good configurations as cut-and-paste examples for system administrators.

User interface design was identified as critical but hard: people who implement encryption are mathematicians and engineers, not usability experts. Simple defaults were seen as crucial: making security features 'on by default' (Mandatory To Use) rather than 'on by default if implemented' (Mandatory To Implement) could have outsized impact. The workshop also highlighted intermediaries like captive portals and firewalls that break end-to-end security. These should be distinguished from active attacks and ideally addressed through new protocols rather than middlebox tricks.
sections.plainLanguage: Good secret codes do not help if nobody turns them on. Laws, clear instructions, and friendly warnings matter. Computers should protect you by default, not make you dig through menus. Even fancy technical tricks do not work if governments do not allow them.

sections.title: Transport and Research Directions
sections.content:
An unofficial transport and routing area break-out identified how lower-layer protocols could help hide metadata. The LEDBAT protocol, designed for bulk transfers that do not mind reordering or delay, could allow applications to spray traffic across multiple paths or vary paths per packet (using IPv6 flow labels or UDP source port variation), making it harder for attackers to capture full conversations. Encryption at layer 3 (IP level) using tunnels or VPNs could hide source and destination addresses.

Several research gaps were identified: the interaction of compression and encryption (shown by the CRIME attack), proactive algorithm deprecation, return-oriented programming defenses, metadata obfuscation, and methods to hide the existence of traffic. The workshop identified a need for better feedback between security research and standardization. Standards bodies should flag open problems, and researchers should share findings more actively with protocol designers.
sections.plainLanguage: Some tricks from the transport layer can scatter your messages across different paths so eavesdroppers cannot reassemble them. Researchers need to tell engineers what is possible and what is still hard, and engineers need to tell researchers what problems they face.
